# Multiplexer

> A lightweight TCP message broker for service-to-service messaging, not a socket multiplexer and not a WebSocket server: request/reply and publish/subscribe between services on a trusted network. Peers connect over TCP, announce a peer type, and exchange typed messages routed by a declarative rules file, with round-robin load balancing, fan-out and automatic failover across active-active instances. Stateless, no single point of failure. C++17 core, C++ and Python client libraries, built with Bazel or with a Makefile.

Vocabulary used everywhere: a peer is a client (keeps control, sends requests or events) or a backend (hands control to the library loop, receives, may answer); both talk to multiplexers. Only a client built on the synchronous `Client` is passive; the threaded and asyncio clients and both backend classes run the loop all the time.

## Facts to know before reading further

- Getting it: a release ships a static `mxcontrol` for any x86_64 Linux, the image `ghcr.io/kulewski/multiplexer:<version>` (distroless, nonroot, port 1980, mount your rules file over /etc/mx/multiplexer.rules), a Debian package per Debian/Ubuntu release with mxcontrol, the C++ library, headers and pkg-config, and manylinux wheels for CPython 3.10 and up (docs/packaging.md); or build from source with Bazel or make (docs/building.md). On Kubernetes: a StatefulSet with one ClusterIP Service per pod, so that every instance has an address that always resolves and never changes; no operator (docs/operations.md).
- Prerequisites: Bazel 6.2.1 through Bazelisk (`.bazelversion`), a C++17 compiler (gcc 11 or newer, clang 18), `protoc` with `libprotobuf` of the same version, Python 3.10 or newer with headers and `python3-protobuf`; Asio, pybind11 and googletest are fetched by Bazel. Verified on clean Debian 12 and 13, Ubuntu 22.04 and 24.04 (docs/building.md). Without Bazel, `make` builds the same from the distribution's Asio, pybind11 (2.9 or newer) and googletest packages.
- Consuming it: declare the repository as `@mx` with `git_repository`, call `mx_dependencies()` then `mx_setup()` in WORKSPACE, point the build at your rules file with `--@mx//:multiplexer_rules=`, depend on `@mx//multiplexer:clients` or `:servers` (Python) and `@mx//multiplexer:client` (C++); tests get `@mx//multiplexer/testing`.
- Semantics: a message is delivered at most once per multiplexer to whoever is connected now, nothing is queued or persisted; a request whose reply is late is sent again to another backend, so a backend may receive a request twice and every attempt has a new id; a request addressed to one instance (`to=`) reaches that instance or fails; order holds per connection, and a lane keeps a stream on one connection; no authentication, for a trusted network (docs/guarantees.md).
- Reserved: peer types and message types 1 to 99 belong to the protocol; deployments use 100 and up in their own rules file, from which the constants are generated (docs/rules.md).
- `is_passive` in the rules file is needed only by peer types built on the synchronous `Client`; ThreadedClient, AsyncClient and both backend classes run the loop all the time. A BaseMultiplexerServer handler must finish within the multiplexer's drop interval (90 s); BaseThreadedMultiplexerServer has no such limit.
